newsitem.title: USA: CME weighs plans to boost currency futures volume.
newsitem.headline: CME weighs plans to boost currency futures volume.

text.p: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange is exploring ways to boost volume in its currency futures products.
"The board believes that any measure to encourage a critical mass of floor traders to remain in the currency pits is a positive action," a bulletin from the board's meeting on Wednesday said.

The board appointed an ad hoc committee to review currency quadrant space. The group, composed of board members, "will explore ways in which to reconfigure the currency pits in order to facilitate business," the bulletin said.
One current plan is to shrink the size of the mark pit, a CME spokeswoman said. The CME in July 1993 expanded currency pits when it shifted the quadrant to its upper trading floor.
That move drew protests from members who complained the new pits were too big and steeply tiered for traders to hear each other and so far apart that currency spreading dried up.
CME will hold member meetings about space in currencies.

The board also said it would ask the Commodity Futures Trading Commssion to let currency traders stand on the top step with brokers. The CME said floor brokers who now stand on the top step will not be displaced from their current locations.
The CME will also ask the CFTC to approve rule amendments to allow off-floor trading terminals for its computerized Large Order Execution (LOX) system, which CME began testing in July.
LOX allows currency orders of 200 contracts or more to be filled electronically at one price, although members involved in the program said no orders have been executed on LOX.
"It has never traded," said one CME currency floor broker.

The board decided to delay funding for the off-floor LOX terminals "given the lack of interest shown in the currency LOX pilot program to date and the relative success of the all-or-nothing pilot program," the bulletin said.
"When the day of the (LOX) pilot program is over, they're probably going to abandon it," the broker added.

"There was no determination made at that meeting to give up on LOX," the CME spokeswoman said. But she said the board decided that spending more money for off-floor LOX terminals at this time would be "premature."
CME does not disclose volume for its all-or-nothing (AON) program, which CME began in June to fill orders of 100 contracts or more in the pit at a single price.
But floor brokers said the AON program has attracted institutional business and handled some sizable trades.
